chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 201 to 210, Kapilar's kurinji decade to the mother (அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து): under the refrain அன்னாய் வாழி வேண்டு அன்னை the friend lays the girl's secret love before her mother through things of his hill, a leaf skirt from his slope, his tufted horses, the muddy water of his land, the gear he wears wet from the rains, and above all his hill itself, whose sight brings the girl tears when hidden and cure when seen.

201.reading: The friend asks the mother, as if idly, what tree it can be on his slope whose golden flowers and gem-like buds my lord himself wore and which became leaf skirts for us as well.
201.nuance: A leaf skirt given by a man is a token of courtship, so the friend's botanical question is a disclosure dressed as ignorance: the flowers belong to his slope and nowhere in theirs, and only the giver can explain them. Whether என்னை is the lover (my lord) or the girl's father decides how bold the hint is.

thinai_evidence.note: the slope of his hill, the kurinji land

comparisons.tenor: the dark gleam of the buds

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; எமக்கும் (for us too) speaks for herself and the girl together, and என்னை (my lord) is read as the hill lord

202.reading: The friend tells the mother that the horses the lord of the tall mountain rode here surely have tufted heads, just like the little Brahmin boy of our town.
202.nuance: The horses are proof that the lord has come to their town (ஊர்ந்த, rode), and the friend lets the mother see them through a homely, laughable likeness, the tufted head of a boy she knows, so the evidence arrives without alarm. மன்ற (surely) marks the friend as having seen them herself.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the tall mountain

comparisons.tenor: the plumed heads of the hill lord's horses

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer

203.reading: The friend tells the mother that the muddy water left over after deer have drunk, in a pit well under leaf litter in his land, is sweeter than the honey-mixed milk of our own garden.
203.nuance: The water is the poorest a hill can offer, dregs that beasts have left in a hole under rotting leaves, and the home drink is the richest; the inversion is the disclosure, for only a heart already given to his land could rank them so. Speaking of tasting it implies she has been, or means to go, there.

thinai_evidence.note: deer and leaf litter of the hill forest

comparisons.tenor: the muddy water of his land

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; the preference may be the girl's own, reported by the friend; the poem does not say whose taste it is

204.reading: The friend asks the mother what it means that, wherever the girl moves among her companions gathered like the mountain nymphs, he gazes at her without pause and says 'she is good, she is good', while to the lord of the mountain I am, alas, the wicked one.
204.nuance: The subject of நோக்கி and என்ப is not named; read with மலை கிழவோற்கு, it is the hill lord who watches and praises, and the friend tells the mother so by complaining that she is the obstacle. Another reading makes the townswomen the watchers.

comparisons.tenor: the girl and her companions in their row

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; தீயேன் is read as the friend's own complaint that she, who keeps guard, is the hindrance in the lover's eyes; it could also be the girl speaking

205.reading: The friend tells the mother that her girl is very modest and fears even her, yet longs to sleep on the broad chest of the lord of the high mountain with its loud white waterfall, and the friend grieves for her.
205.nuance: The friend explains why she, not the girl, is speaking: the girl's shame and her fear of her mother keep her silent, so the disclosure must come from a second mouth. The two halves, great shame and open desire, are set side by side without a 'but', as the girl holds both at once.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl's longing for union with the hill lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; என் தோழி names the girl as the speaker's friend

206.reading: The friend bids the mother look there: he is like a watchman of the rainy hill, his bright sword wet in its strap from the spray, his great anklet ringed with moss, his striped belt beaded with cold dew.
206.nuance: Every detail of his gear is a record of nights spent out in the wet hill: spray on the sword, moss grown on the anklet from wading, dew settled on the belt. The friend lets the mother read his constancy from his clothes, and the likeness to a field watchman makes the stranger look like one of their own hill people.

comparisons.tenor: the hill lord standing wet with his gear

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; உவக்காண் (look there) points the mother to the man himself

207.reading: The friend asks the mother whether her millet is not drying at all, and bids her look: his tall gem-dark hill shows with rain cloud on its head like a wrapping of caul fat.
207.nuance: Whether உணங்கல means the millet will not dry because rain is coming from his hill, or that it is withering for want of rain that his hill's cloud promises, the friend turns the mother's eye from her crop to his hill; on the second reading the drying millet stands for the pining girl, as the Kalittokai says openly, but no stated situation anchors that pairing, so it is not tagged ullurai. வழுக்கு as the sense of the fat-wrapped likeness is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet crop and the hill

comparisons.tenor: the white cloud wrapped round the hill's head
the dark blue of his hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer

208.reading: The friend tells the mother that whenever the gem-coloured great mountain of his land, where golden new vengai flowers fill the deep pits the hunters dug for tubers, is hidden from view, the girl's long flower-like eyes fill with tears.
208.nuance: The vengai's golden bloom is the kurinji sign of the wedding season, and its flowers filling the hollows the hunters left can be felt as a promise that his land is ready; but no second correspondence or stated situation completes it, so it stays scene. The girl weeps not when he is away but when his hill is out of sight, so the sight of the land stands in for the man.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai tree and the hill hunters

comparisons.tenor: the blue of the far mountain

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; இவள் (this girl) is pointed out to the mother

209.reading: If you want me to forget him, the speaker tells her, his tall gem-dark hill never stops appearing, crowned with a white-headed dark cloud like the flower of the bean that blooms in the east wind.
209.nuance: She does not refuse to forget; she says the landscape will not let her, putting the cause outside herself. The white-topped dark cloud is a bean flower in the cold east-wind season, so the image also tells the time of year, when the hill is most often cloud-crowned and so most often seen.

comparisons.tenor: the white-headed dark cloud on his hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; but யான் அவர் மறத்தல் (that I forget him) makes the girl the speaker here, answering one who urges her to forget; அன்னை may be the friend, as the address often is, or the mother herself

210.reading: The friend tells the mother that the girl's sickness might abate, and her gem-like bright jewels stay in place, if she climbed the flesh-smelling boulder in our garden and stood looking at the flowering hill of his land.
210.nuance: Jewels that stay in place mean a body that is no longer wasting, since slipping bangles are love-sickness's sign; the friend prescribes the cure while naming its source, his land, so the remedy is itself the disclosure. The boulder smells of flesh from the hunters' kills dried on it.

thinai_evidence.note: the boulder and the flowering hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; அவள் உற்ற நோய் speaks of the girl in the third person to the mother

links.note: In Natrinai 359 the friend says the hill lord gave them a leaf skirt (உடுக்கும் தழை) that they dare not wear for fear of the mother nor return for fear of hurting him; in Ainkurunuru 201 the leaves have become their skirts (எமக்கும் தழையாயின) and the friend asks the mother what tree on his slope they come from.
links.teaches: The leaf skirt that in Natrinai is a gift too dangerous to wear before the mother becomes in the Ainkurunuru the very thing the friend shows her, so the pair traces one courtship token from the secret it endangers to the disclosure it carries.

links.note: In Natrinai 53 the mother herself says the new stream water coming down from the high hill is medicine and sends the girl to drink and bathe in it; in Ainkurunuru 203 the friend tells the mother that the muddy water of his land is sweeter than their honeyed milk.
links.teaches: The mother who prescribes the water of the far hill without knowing whose hill it is, and the friend who tells her that the water of his land is sweeter than home's milk, together show that in kurinji the lover's water stands for the lover, so the disclosure turns the mother's innocent remedy into a confession.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 356 the foster mother grieves that the girl who refused milk mixed with puffed rice must now gulp scalding muddy water (கலுழி) by a dried spring; in Ainkurunuru 203 the girl's side says the muddy water (கலிழி) of his land is sweeter than honeyed milk.
links.teaches: The two poems make opposite claims about the same exchange of home's milk for the forest's muddy water, a pitiable loss to the foster mother and a gain to the girl's side, which shows that the pathos of the elopement poems is the mother's view and not the girl's.

links.note: In Akananuru 272 the mother sees the night visitor wet from the hill, garlanded with koothalam, and takes him for Murugu, scattering millet in worship; in Ainkurunuru 206 the friend shows the mother a man wet with spray and dew and likens him to a watchman of the rainy hill.
links.teaches: Where the mother left to herself reads the drenched visitor from the hill as a god, the friend who discloses the love names him as a man like their own field watchmen, so the disclosure works by bringing the stranger down from the sacred to the familiar.

links.note: In Akananuru 378 the deserted girl says she lives only because the peak of his hill, crowned with a waterfall, is in sight (வான்தோய் சிமையம் தோன்றலானே); in Ainkurunuru 209 she says she cannot forget him because his cloud-crowned hill never stops appearing (தோன்றல் அனாது).
links.teaches: The same visible peak is what keeps the girl alive in the Akananuru and what defeats any demand that she forget in the Ainkurunuru, so together they show the hill working as a bond that neither absence nor counsel can loosen.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 367 the friend tells the girl that her shoulders may regain their beauty now that his hill with its cool boulders (துறுகல்) shows after the rain; in Ainkurunuru 210 the friend tells the mother the girl's sickness may abate if she climbs their boulder (துறுகல்) and looks at his hill.
links.teaches: The sight of his hill, offered privately as comfort to the girl in the Kuruntokai, becomes in the Ainkurunuru a cure the friend asks the mother to allow, so the pair shows a consolation turned into an open request that names its source.

links.note: In 208 the girl's eyes fill with tears whenever his mountain is hidden; in 210 the friend says her sickness may abate if she stands looking at his hill.
links.teaches: Read together the two poems make the girl's state a function of the hill's visibility, tears when it is hidden and healing when it is seen, which is the argument the friend needs before the mother for letting the girl climb and look.

links.note: Both open on the same refrain to the mother and point to the lover's mount: in the neythal decade the shore lord's chariot is the medicine for the girl's sickness, in the kurinji decade the hill lord's horses have tufted heads like the town's Brahmin boy.
links.teaches: The two disclosure decades present the lover's mount to the mother as evidence in opposite tones, the neythal friend solemnly as a cure and the kurinji friend comically through a homely likeness, so the same act of disclosure could be made by gravity or by disarming laughter.

source_issues: 201-210: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the refrain and the decade title.
209: the refrain's addressee and the speaker are unclear; யான் அவர் மறத்தல் makes the girl the speaker, against the friend-to-mother frame of the decade.
204: the subject of நோக்கி and என்ப is unstated, and தீயேன் may be the friend's or the girl's word; the sense of the poem turns on it.
207: உணங்கல கொல்லோ (drying or withering) and நிணம்பொதி வழுக்கில் are obscure; the readings are uncertain.
201: என்னை may be 'my lord' (the lover) or 'my father'.
203, 204, 205, 206, 208, 210: the shown text carries repaired lines (flags in show); the readings follow the repaired text.
